Couldn't it be possible that our idea that leads to "there must be something else to explain this gravitational pull" also just point to "our understanding of a gravitational pull has a flaw"

Is there more to think that something like dark matter exists?

Yes, in fact there is.

The distribution of dark matter of distant galaxies can be indirectly observed to be different than that of normal matter, thanks to our understanding of how matter affects gravity due to general relativity. If we assume that the gravity that binds galaxies together is due ONLY to the matter that we can see, then we expect the more central parts of galaxies to rotate much faster around the center than the outside. I use the example of out own solar system, where the inner planets have orbital periods of less than 2 yrs, and all the outer planets upwards of 8 to hundreds of years.

With galaxies however, what we observe is that the outer regions of the galaxy orbit the center in much closer to equal proportion to the center most regions. This we could attribute to unseen matter, aka dark matter.

What's more, is that thanks to general relativity (where matter bends spacetime and spacetime informs matter's motion) we see distant galaxies bending light in ways more extreme than we should expect from the amount of matter than we can see. This we can also attribute to unseen matter. BUT, most importantly, we can measure WHERE this unseen matter is located within such galaxies or galaxy clusters. More importantly, taking dark matter into account in our computer models of the universe dramatically improves the accuracy of these simulations, assuming dark matter responds to gravity in the same way.

TL;DR we can't see dark matter, but with lots of math and computers, we can map out where it should be, and it makes more sense to assume it does exist than to assume its effects are caused by something else.
